**Modulus** Rewrite the divisibility in modular form  

\[
(2^{n}-1)\%7=0\;\Longleftrightarrow\;7\mid 2^{n}-1\;\Longleftrightarrow\;2^{n}\equiv1\pmod 7 .
\]

**Witness** A single power gives the modulus  

\[
2^{3}=8\equiv1\pmod7\qquad\text{(since }2^{3}-1=7\text{)} .
\]

**Identity** From the witness, powers of the triple give the same residue  

\[
(2^{3})^{k}\equiv1^{k}\pmod7\;\Longrightarrow\;2^{3k}\equiv1\pmod7\qquad(k\in\mathbb N).
\]

**Bound** Write \(n\) by Euclidean division by 3:  

\[
n=3q+r,\qquad 0\le r<3\;(r=n\bmod 3).
\]

Then  

\[
2^{n}=2^{3q+r}= (2^{3})^{q}\,2^{r}\equiv1\cdot2^{r}\equiv2^{r}\pmod7 .
\]

**Case split** Check the three possible remainders:

\[
\begin{aligned}
r=0&:\;2^{0}=1\equiv1\pmod7,\\
r=1&:\;2^{1}=2\not\equiv1\pmod7,\\
r=2&:\;2^{2}=4\not\equiv1\pmod7.
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus \(2^{r}\equiv1\pmod7\) iff \(r=0\).

**Conclusion** \(2^{n}\equiv1\pmod7\) iff the remainder \(r\) is 0, i.e. iff \(3\mid n\). Hence  

\[

**Modulus.**  
\(7\mid 2^{n}-1\)  ⇔  \(2^{n}\equiv 1\pmod 7\)  ⇔  \(2^{n}\bmod 7 =1\).

**Witness.**  
\(2^{3}=8\equiv 1\pmod 7\); hence \(\;2^{3}\bmod 7 =1\).

**Identity.**  
By the given lemma \(h_{\text{mod\_val}}\),

\[
2^{n}\bmod 7 = 2^{\,n\bmod 3}\bmod 7 .
\]

**Case split.**  
From \(h_{\text{cases}}\) we have the three possibilities for \(r:=n\bmod 3\):

* \(r=0\): \(2^{r}\bmod 7 =2^{0}\bmod 7 =1\) – compatible with the modulus.
* \(r=1\): \(2^{r}\bmod 7 =2^{1}\bmod 7 =2\neq1\) – contradicts \(2^{n}\bmod 7 =1\).
* \(r=2\): \(2^{r}\bmod 7 =2^{2}\bmod 7 =4\neq1\) – likewise a contradiction.

Thus the only viable case is \(r=0\); i.e. \(n\bmod 3 =0\).

**Bound (conclusion).**  
\(n\bmod 3 =0\) is equivalent to \(3\mid n\). Hence  

\[
7\mid 2^{n}-1\;\Longrightarrow\;3\mid n .
\]

\(7\mid 2^{n}-1\)  ⇔  \(2^{n}\equiv 1\pmod 7\)  ⇔  \(2^{n}\bmod 7 =1\).
